Its action handler should only update a copied dictionary in memory and should refuse any request that is not in an explicit allowlist. It must not import subprocess, call a shell, open a socket, write a file, inspect a real process list, alter a registry, or invoke a system management API. Before each simulated change, emit a structured event containing a training timestamp, actor name, target service, requested action, previous state, and resulting state. Have the detector flag a protected service being stopped, a startup mode changing from automatic to disabled, logging being altered, several security-control requests in a short window, or an exclusion being added immediately after a failed login. Recovery can restore the last trusted snapshot, rotate the simulated host credential, remove the fake exclusion, restart the fake logging service, and generate a report showing every rejected and accepted action. To make the scenario engaging, give students a timeline in which the fake virus first stops the mock antivirus, then changes its startup setting, then tries to erase telemetry; ask them to identify the earliest high-confidence alert and choose containment before recovery. End with a mapping from each simulated event to the real telemetry an incident responder would seek, such as endpoint service events, policy changes, and tamper alerts. This teaches behavior, detection, and recovery while ensuring the code cannot disable protection on the student's computer or any other machine.
